name: Hydrogen
blurb: The lightest element and the most abundant substance in the universe — three quarters of all ordinary matter.
funFact: Every water molecule in your body carries hydrogen forged in the first minutes after the Big Bang.

name: Helium
blurb: An inert noble gas so light it escapes Earth's gravity and leaks steadily into space.
funFact: Helium was found in the Sun's spectrum 27 years before anyone isolated it on Earth.
appearance: colorless gas, exhibiting a red-orange glow when placed in a high-voltage electric field

name: Lithium
blurb: The lightest metal — soft enough to cut with a knife, and the heart of every rechargeable battery.
funFact: The lithium in your phone is older than the Earth. Most of it was made in the Big Bang.

name: Beryllium
blurb: A stiff, ultralight metal used in aerospace mirrors and X-ray windows. Highly toxic as dust.
funFact: The James Webb telescope's 18 mirror segments are beryllium — it barely flexes at −230 °C.

name: Boron
blurb: A metalloid that toughens glass. Borosilicate cookware and fiberglass both depend on it.
funFact: Boron is rare in the cosmos because stars destroy it. Cosmic rays shattering heavier atoms make most of it.

name: Carbon
blurb: The backbone of every known living thing — and the same element in both graphite and diamond.
funFact: Carbon forms more compounds than all other elements combined: over ten million and counting.

name: Nitrogen
blurb: Seventy-eight percent of the air you breathe, and locked into every protein and strand of DNA.
funFact: Pulling nitrogen out of the air to make fertilizer now feeds roughly half the people alive.

name: Oxygen
blurb: The element that made animal life possible, and nearly half the mass of Earth's crust.
funFact: Earth's oxygen is a waste product. Cyanobacteria dumped it into the air and caused a mass extinction.

name: Fluorine
blurb: The most reactive element there is. It attacks almost everything, including glass and water.
funFact: Fluorine is aggressive enough to burn asbestos — yet bonded into Teflon it becomes nearly inert.

name: Neon
blurb: A noble gas that glows a distinct orange-red when electrified. The original neon sign.
funFact: Every color other than orange-red in a 'neon' sign comes from a different gas or a coating.
appearance: colorless gas exhibiting an orange-red glow when placed in a high voltage electric field

name: Sodium
blurb: A soft metal that fizzes violently in water. One half of ordinary table salt.
funFact: Your nerves fire by pumping sodium across cell membranes. Thought runs on this metal.

name: Magnesium
blurb: A light structural metal — and the single atom at the center of chlorophyll.
funFact: Every green leaf on Earth is green because of a magnesium atom catching sunlight.

name: Aluminium
blurb: The most abundant metal in the crust, yet it was once more precious than gold.
funFact: Aluminum was so hard to refine that Napoleon III served his most honored guests on aluminum plates.

name: Silicon
blurb: The metalloid of sand, glass, and every microchip in the modern world.
funFact: A finished silicon wafer is purer than almost anything else humans make: 99.9999999% silicon.

name: Phosphorus
blurb: Essential to DNA and ATP. One of its forms ignites on contact with air.
funFact: Phosphorus was first isolated from boiled-down urine, and it glows in the dark — hence 'light-bearer'.
appearance: colourless, waxy white, yellow, scarlet, red, violet, black

name: Sulfur
blurb: A yellow nonmetal of volcanoes and vulcanized rubber, notorious for its smell.
funFact: Sulfur is one of the few elements the ancients found pure in the ground: the 'brimstone' of scripture.

name: Chlorine
blurb: A choking green gas that, bonded to sodium, becomes something you sprinkle on food.
funFact: Chlorinating drinking water may be the single largest life-saving intervention in public health history.

name: Argon
blurb: The third most common gas in the atmosphere, and a cheap inert shield for welding.
funFact: Argon fills the gap in double-glazed windows because it conducts heat worse than air does.
appearance: colorless gas exhibiting a lilac/violet glow when placed in a high voltage electric field

name: Potassium
blurb: A reactive alkali metal that your nerves and muscles cannot work without.
funFact: Bananas are faintly radioactive: a fraction of all natural potassium is the isotope K-40.

name: Calcium
blurb: The metal of bone, shell, and limestone. Fifth most abundant element in the crust.
funFact: The white cliffs of Dover are the compressed skeletons of trillions of microscopic algae.

name: Scandium
blurb: A light, rare transition metal used in high-end bicycle frames and stadium lamps.
funFact: Mendeleev predicted scandium from a gap in his table years before anyone found it.

name: Titanium
blurb: As strong as steel at half the weight, and unbothered by seawater or the human body.
funFact: Titanium is so biocompatible that bone will grow directly onto an implant and bond with it.

name: Vanadium
blurb: A hardening additive that makes tool steel tough. Also a promising flow-battery metal.
funFact: Its salts run through nearly every color of the rainbow depending on oxidation state.

name: Chromium
blurb: The metal behind stainless steel's shine and its refusal to rust.
funFact: Chromium gives rubies their red and emeralds their green. Same atom, different crystal.

name: Manganese
blurb: A hard, brittle metal that makes steel resistant to shattering under impact.
funFact: Manganese dioxide is the reason the alkaline battery in your drawer works at all.

name: Iron
blurb: The most-used metal on Earth, and the core of the planet itself.
funFact: Iron is where fusion stops paying. A star that reaches iron has minutes left before it collapses.
appearance: lustrous metallic with a grayish tinge

name: Cobalt
blurb: A magnetic metal of deep-blue pigments and lithium-ion cathodes.
funFact: Cobalt blue has colored Chinese porcelain and Egyptian glass for over two thousand years.

name: Nickel
blurb: A corrosion-resistant metal found in coins, stainless steel, and battery chemistry.
funFact: Most 'nickels' are mostly copper. The coin is only a quarter nickel.
appearance: lustrous, metallic, and silver with a gold tinge

name: Copper
blurb: The first metal humans ever smelted, and still the default conductor of electricity.
funFact: The Statue of Liberty is copper, 2.4 mm thick — and green because it oxidized.

name: Zinc
blurb: The sacrificial coating that stops steel from rusting, and an essential trace nutrient.
funFact: Galvanized steel survives by letting the zinc corrode instead. The coating dies for the metal.

name: Gallium
blurb: A metal that melts in your hand, and the basis of LEDs and fast radio chips.
funFact: Gallium melts at 30 °C. A spoon made of it dissolves in a cup of tea.

name: Germanium
blurb: The metalloid of the first transistors, now used in fiber optics and infrared lenses.
funFact: The first transistor, in 1947, was germanium. Silicon took over a decade later.

name: Arsenic
blurb: A metalloid infamous as a poison, now quietly essential to semiconductors.
funFact: Arsenic was the poison of choice for so long that it was nicknamed 'inheritance powder'.

name: Selenium
blurb: A trace nutrient, and the photoconductor that made photocopying possible.
funFact: Early photocopiers coated a drum in selenium: it conducts electricity only where light hits it.
appearance: black, red, and gray (not pictured) allotropes

name: Bromine
blurb: The only nonmetal that is liquid at room temperature. Heavy, fuming, red-brown.
funFact: Ancient Tyrian purple came from sea snails, and its color comes from bromine.

name: Krypton
blurb: A noble gas used in high-performance lighting — and once in the definition of the meter.
funFact: From 1960 to 1983 the meter was officially defined by the wavelength of krypton-86 light.
appearance: colorless gas, exhibiting a whitish glow in a high electric field

name: Rubidium
blurb: A soft alkali metal so reactive it ignites in air. Used in atomic clocks.
funFact: Rubidium clocks are the workhorses that keep GPS satellites honest.

name: Strontium
blurb: The metal that makes fireworks red — and a bone-seeker when radioactive.
funFact: Strontium-90 from 1950s bomb tests is still detectable in the teeth of people born then.

name: Yttrium
blurb: A rare-earth metal found in phosphors, lasers, and high-temperature superconductors.
funFact: The red phosphor in old color televisions was an yttrium compound.

name: Zirconium
blurb: A corrosion-proof metal that lines nuclear fuel rods and imitates diamond as cubic zirconia.
funFact: Zirconium is nearly transparent to neutrons, which is why reactor cores are built with it.

name: Niobium
blurb: A superconducting metal used in MRI magnets and jet-engine alloys.
funFact: The magnet inside an MRI scanner is niobium wire, kept colder than deep space.

name: Molybdenum
blurb: A high-melting metal that keeps steel strong at extreme temperature.
funFact: Some bacteria use molybdenum to crack nitrogen out of the air — nature's own fertilizer plant.

name: Technetium
blurb: The lightest element with no stable isotope. Made in reactors, not mined.
funFact: Technetium was the first element ever created artificially. It now appears in 30 million medical scans a year.

name: Ruthenium
blurb: A hard platinum-group metal used in electrical contacts and industrial catalysis.
funFact: A ruthenium tip is what makes a good fountain pen nib last a lifetime.

name: Rhodium
blurb: The catalytic metal in your car's exhaust, and often the most expensive of all.
funFact: Rhodium has traded at several times the price of gold. It is rarer than platinum.

name: Palladium
blurb: A platinum-group metal that soaks up hydrogen like a sponge.
funFact: Palladium can absorb over 900 times its own volume in hydrogen gas.

name: Silver
blurb: The best electrical and thermal conductor of any element, and an ancient antimicrobial.
funFact: Photography ran on silver for 150 years. Every negative was silver grains turning dark.

name: Cadmium
blurb: A soft, toxic metal once everywhere in pigments and rechargeable batteries.
funFact: Cadmium yellow gave the Impressionists their brightest sunlight — and slowly poisoned the painters.

name: Indium
blurb: A soft metal whose oxide makes touchscreens both transparent and conductive.
funFact: Every phone screen you have ever tapped had a nearly invisible indium film reading your finger.

name: Tin
blurb: The metal that turned copper into bronze and started an age.
funFact: Cold turns tin into a crumbling gray powder. Church organ pipes have been destroyed by 'tin pest'.

name: Antimony
blurb: A metalloid used in flame retardants and, historically, in cosmetics.
funFact: Egyptian kohl eyeliner was antimony sulfide — the same compound now used to stop fires spreading.

name: Tellurium
blurb: A scarce metalloid used in thin-film solar panels and thermoelectric generators.
funFact: Tellurium is rarer than platinum here yet common in the universe. Earth lost most of its share.

name: Iodine
blurb: A dark violet halogen the thyroid cannot work without. A purple vapor when warmed.
funFact: Adding iodine to table salt eliminated an entire category of preventable brain damage.
appearance: lustrous metallic gray, violet as a gas

name: Xenon
blurb: A heavy noble gas used in brilliant arc lamps — and as a general anesthetic.
funFact: Xenon can put you under with almost no side effects. It is simply far too expensive to use.
appearance: colorless gas, exhibiting a blue glow when placed in a high voltage electric field

name: Cesium
blurb: The most reactive metal on the table. It explodes in water, and it defines the second.
funFact: One second is officially 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a cesium atom.

name: Barium
blurb: A dense alkaline-earth metal whose sulfate is the 'barium meal' of X-ray imaging.
funFact: Barium sulfate is safe to swallow only because it refuses to dissolve. The free ion is toxic.

name: Lanthanum
blurb: The first lanthanide, used in camera lenses and nickel-metal-hydride batteries.
funFact: The battery pack in a first-generation Prius held about 10 kg of lanthanum.

name: Cerium
blurb: The most abundant rare earth, used in catalytic converters and glass polish.
funFact: The spark in a cigarette lighter is cerium alloy shaving off and igniting in air.

name: Praseodymium
blurb: A rare earth in powerful magnets, and in the yellow-green glass of welding goggles.
funFact: Welders' goggles are praseodymium-doped: it blocks the exact yellow glare of molten metal.

name: Neodymium
blurb: The metal behind the strongest permanent magnets ever made.
funFact: Your headphones, hard drive, and every EV motor use neodymium magnets. They hold a thousand times their own weight.

name: Promethium
blurb: The only radioactive lanthanide with no stable isotope. Essentially absent from nature.
funFact: There is thought to be less than a kilogram of promethium in the entire Earth's crust.

name: Samarium
blurb: A rare earth in heat-resistant magnets that keep working past 300 °C.
funFact: Samarium-cobalt magnets fly in spacecraft because they do not weaken when they get hot.

name: Europium
blurb: The rare earth behind the red and blue phosphors in screens and lighting.
funFact: Euro banknotes glow red under UV thanks to a europium compound — a forgery check built into the paper.

name: Gadolinium
blurb: A rare earth used as an MRI contrast agent and as a neutron absorber.
funFact: Gadolinium injected before an MRI makes tumors light up by disturbing the water molecules around them.

name: Terbium
blurb: A rare earth in green phosphors and in materials that change shape in a magnetic field.
funFact: Terbium alloys physically deform in a magnetic field — enough to turn a tabletop into a loudspeaker.

name: Dysprosium
blurb: The additive that stops neodymium magnets from failing when they get hot.
funFact: Without a few percent dysprosium, an electric car's motor magnet would demagnetize itself.

name: Holmium
blurb: The most magnetic element. Used in surgical lasers and magnet pole pieces.
funFact: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any element. It sits at the core of the strongest lab magnets.

name: Erbium
blurb: The rare earth that makes long-haul fiber-optic internet possible.
funFact: Erbium amplifiers boost light directly, without converting it to electricity. The internet's quiet miracle.

name: Thulium
blurb: The rarest stable lanthanide. Used in portable X-ray sources and lasers.
funFact: Thulium is so scarce that it was once priced by the milligram.

name: Ytterbium
blurb: A rare earth at the heart of the most accurate clocks ever built.
funFact: An ytterbium lattice clock would drift less than one second over the age of the universe.

name: Lutetium
blurb: The last lanthanide. Dense, expensive, and used in PET scanner detectors.
funFact: Lutetium crystals turn gamma rays into flashes of visible light. They are the eyes of a PET scanner.

name: Hafnium
blurb: A refractory metal used in reactor control rods and in modern chip insulation.
funFact: Hafnium oxide replaced silicon dioxide inside transistors around 2007 and rescued Moore's law.

name: Tantalum
blurb: A dense, inert metal that forms the tiny capacitors inside every phone.
funFact: Tantalum is inert enough for surgical implants and dense enough to shape an explosive charge.

name: Tungsten
blurb: The highest melting point of any metal: 3,422 °C. The original lightbulb filament.
funFact: Tungsten carbide is hard enough to drill through rock and to cut other metals.

name: Rhenium
blurb: One of the rarest metals in the crust. Used in jet-engine turbine blades.
funFact: Rhenium has the second-highest melting point of all elements, and no ore of its own.

name: Osmium
blurb: The densest naturally occurring element — twice the density of lead.
funFact: A liter of osmium weighs 22.6 kg. Its oxide, meanwhile, will blind you.

name: Iridium
blurb: Nearly as dense as osmium, and the most corrosion-resistant metal known.
funFact: A worldwide iridium layer in the rock marks the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.

name: Platinum
blurb: A precious catalytic metal found in fuel cells, chemotherapy, and exhaust systems.
funFact: Cisplatin, a platinum drug, cures most testicular cancer. One of oncology's great successes.

name: Gold
blurb: The metal that never tarnishes. Humanity's store of value for six thousand years.
funFact: Every gold atom was forged in a neutron-star collision, then delivered here by asteroid impacts.

name: Mercury
blurb: The only metal liquid at room temperature, and a potent neurotoxin.
funFact: Hat makers used mercury to felt fur, and it damaged their nerves — hence 'mad as a hatter'.

name: Thallium
blurb: A soft, highly toxic metal once sold as rat poison, now used in infrared optics.
funFact: Thallium poisoning is nearly symptomless at first, which made it a favorite of poisoners.

name: Lead
blurb: Dense, soft, and toxic. The end point of most radioactive decay chains.
funFact: Roman plumbing was lead. The word 'plumber' comes from plumbum, its Latin name.

name: Bismuth
blurb: A brittle heavy metal, remarkably non-toxic, that grows spectacular rainbow crystals.
funFact: Bismuth is the heaviest practically non-toxic element. It is the active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol.

name: Polonium
blurb: An intensely radioactive metalloid. A gram would glow and boil its own container.
funFact: Polonium-210 is roughly 250,000 times more toxic than hydrogen cyanide by weight.

name: Astatine
blurb: The rarest naturally occurring element. Perhaps 25 grams exist in the whole crust.
funFact: Astatine has never been seen in bulk. A visible sample would vaporize from its own radioactivity.

name: Radon
blurb: A radioactive noble gas that seeps up out of rock and collects in basements.
funFact: Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking — and it is invisible and odorless.
appearance: colorless gas, occasionally glows green or red in discharge tubes

name: Francium
blurb: The second-rarest element, with a half-life measured in minutes.
funFact: No more than 30 grams of francium exist in the Earth's crust at any given moment.

name: Radium
blurb: A radioactive alkaline-earth metal that glows faintly blue in the dark.
funFact: Radium watch dials poisoned the women who painted them. The 'Radium Girls' won landmark labor rights.

name: Actinium
blurb: The first actinide. Intensely radioactive, and glowing pale blue.
funFact: Actinium-225 is now used to deliver alpha particles directly into cancer cells.

name: Thorium
blurb: A weakly radioactive metal, three times more abundant than uranium.
funFact: Thorium reactors are periodically hailed as the future of nuclear power, and periodically shelved.

name: Protactinium
blurb: A dense, scarce actinide with no application outside the research lab.
funFact: Protactinium is so troublesome to purify that only about 125 grams has ever been extracted.

name: Uranium
blurb: The heaviest primordial element, and the fuel of both nuclear power and weapons.
funFact: Uranium glass fluoresces bright green under UV. Victorian households ate off mildly radioactive plates.

name: Neptunium
blurb: The first synthetic transuranic element, named for the planet past Uranus.
funFact: Neptunium was made in 1940 and named to continue the planetary sequence beyond uranium.

name: Plutonium
blurb: A synthetic metal that powers spacecraft and warheads alike.
funFact: Voyager 1 has run on plutonium-238 heat since 1977 and is now outside the solar system.
appearance: silvery white, tarnishing to dark gray in air

name: Americium
blurb: A synthetic actinide sitting inside millions of homes — in smoke detectors.
funFact: Your smoke alarm holds a speck of americium. Its radiation is what actually senses the smoke.

name: Curium
blurb: A synthetic actinide that glows in the dark from its own radioactivity.
funFact: Curium runs hot enough to serve as a power source, and it self-illuminates purple.
appearance: silvery metallic, glows purple in the dark

name: Berkelium
blurb: A synthetic element produced only in milligram quantities, ever.
funFact: Berkelium was the target used to synthesize tennessine. Element 117 exists because of it.

name: Californium
blurb: A synthetic neutron source used to start reactors and to prospect for gold.
funFact: A microgram of californium emits 170 million neutrons a minute. It costs about $27 million per gram.

name: Einsteinium
blurb: Discovered in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb test.
funFact: Einsteinium was found in debris from the 1952 Ivy Mike test, and kept classified for years.

name: Fermium
blurb: The heaviest element that can be made in bulk by neutron bombardment.
funFact: Past fermium, elements must be built by smashing nuclei together one atom at a time.

name: Mendelevium
blurb: A synthetic element made a single atom at a time in particle accelerators.
funFact: Mendelevium honors the man who left gaps in his table for elements nobody had found yet.

name: Nobelium
blurb: A synthetic actinide whose discovery was disputed for more than a decade.
funFact: Three separate labs claimed nobelium. The naming fight lasted far longer than the element does.

name: Lawrencium
blurb: The last actinide, existing only for hours at a time inside a laboratory.
funFact: Lawrencium's electron configuration was measured only in 2015, and it breaks the expected pattern.

name: Rutherfordium
blurb: The first transactinide. A few atoms at a time, lasting seconds.
funFact: Rutherfordium sat at the center of a Cold War naming dispute between Berkeley and Dubna.

name: Dubnium
blurb: A synthetic superheavy element named for the Russian lab that helped find it.
funFact: Dubnium's name was the peace treaty that ended the 'Transfermium Wars'.

name: Seaborgium
blurb: A superheavy element named after a living scientist — the first time that happened.
funFact: Seaborgium broke the convention against naming elements for the living, and started a rules fight.

name: Bohrium
blurb: A synthetic element with a half-life measured in seconds.
funFact: Only a few dozen atoms of bohrium have ever existed.

name: Hassium
blurb: A superheavy element, probably a dense metal, known from a handful of atoms.
funFact: Hassium's chemistry has actually been studied — from about ten atoms, one at a time.

name: Meitnerium
blurb: A synthetic element too short-lived for its properties to be measured directly.
funFact: Meitnerium honors Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission and was denied the Nobel for it.

name: Darmstadtium
blurb: A superheavy element whose longest-lived isotope survives about ten seconds.
funFact: Darmstadtium was made by firing nickel at lead for a week to produce a single atom.

name: Roentgenium
blurb: A synthetic element predicted to be a noble, gold-like metal.
funFact: Roentgenium sits directly beneath gold, and is predicted to be even less reactive than it.

name: Copernicium
blurb: A superheavy element that may be a volatile liquid, like the mercury above it.
funFact: Copernicium might be a gas at room temperature — if anyone could collect enough to check.

name: Nihonium
blurb: The first element discovered by a Japanese research team.
funFact: Nihonium took RIKEN nine years of continuous bombardment to produce three atoms.

name: Flerovium
blurb: A superheavy element that appears to behave oddly like a noble gas.
funFact: Flerovium sits under lead but seems barely reactive. Relativity distorts its electrons that much.

name: Moscovium
blurb: A synthetic element that exists for fractions of a second.
funFact: Moscovium became briefly famous when a conspiracy theorist claimed UFOs were fueled by element 115.

name: Livermorium
blurb: A superheavy element named for the Livermore national laboratory.
funFact: Livermorium decays in about 60 milliseconds — barely time to confirm that it existed.

name: Tennessine
blurb: One of the newest elements, built from berkelium and calcium.
funFact: Tennessine needed a berkelium target so rare that only one lab on Earth could supply it.

name: Oganesson
blurb: The heaviest element ever made. The bottom-right corner of the table.
funFact: Oganesson should be a noble gas, but calculations suggest it is actually a reactive solid.
